article.overview: A cellular radiation response experiment measures how living cells change when they are exposed to ionising radiation, especially the damage that radiation causes to DNA and the cell's ability to repair that damage and keep growing. The catalogue entry describes a class of biological experiments rather than one standard instrument. The best-documented flown example identified in this research is BioSentinel, a 6U CubeSat that carried budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) as a radiation biosensor on NASA's Artemis I mission, launched on 16 November 2022 [1][2]. Yeast is a single-celled organism, not a mammalian cell culture, so its results cannot be transferred directly to human cells. The research did not find published deep-space biological results from the flight [1][4].
article.description: Cellular radiation response experiments expose living cells, or a model organism made of cells, to a radiation environment and then measure a biological readout such as growth, metabolism, survival or DNA-repair activity. Each biological measurement is paired with a physical measurement of the radiation delivered. Ground experiments usually use particle accelerators to control dose and particle type, whereas flight experiments must measure the radiation environment the cells actually experience. The payload therefore has two linked parts: a biological sample system that keeps the cells viable and measurable, and a radiation sensor that records dose and particle type. The BioSentinel design, the best-documented flown example here, pairs dried yeast on microfluidic cards with an optical growth-and-metabolism readout and a linear energy transfer (LET) spectrometer [1][3].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of this class of experiment is to determine how biological systems respond to radiation types and doses that cannot be fully reproduced on Earth, particularly the mixed particle environment beyond Earth's magnetosphere. For BioSentinel, NASA states that the mission aims to measure how space radiation affects living organisms over long durations beyond low Earth orbit, and describes it as the first study of biological radiation response beyond low Earth orbit in almost 50 years [1]. Ground work preceded the flight. In a 2023 Astrobiology paper, desiccated wild-type and rad51-deletion yeast were irradiated with 1 GeV protons at NASA's Space Radiation Laboratory at 0, 10 or 250 cGy. Both strains showed a dose-dependent drop in alamarBlue reduction, a metabolic readout, starting at 10 cGy, and the rad51-deletion strain, which lacks a double-strand-break repair gene, responded more strongly [3]. The authors attribute the stronger response to the repair defect but did not directly measure DNA damage, so that link is an inference [3]. Intended applications are mainly radiation-risk assessment for future crews and testing of countermeasures; the sources reviewed do not quantify these applications.
article.operating_principle: In the BioSentinel design, yeast is stored dry on microfluidic cards and activated at set points during the mission [1]. Each card well holds about 100 microlitres with roughly 10^5 cells per well, and the cards sit in two nine-card fluidic manifolds [3]. Growth and metabolism are read optically with a three-colour LED source and detector and a metabolic indicator dye [1][3]. A TimePix-based spectrometer measures linear energy transfer (LET), which describes how densely a particle deposits energy along its path; high-LET particles tend to cause more clustered damage. The spectrometer also records total ionising dose [1][3]. Comparing the biological change with the measured radiation environment, and with identical Earth-based control payloads, is what turns an observation into a dose-response relationship [1]. Heaters keep the payload at or above 4 degrees C, and desiccant chambers control humidity; no active cooling is described [3].
article.scientific_importance: Cellular radiation response data link the physics of the radiation environment to biological effect. Ground experiments can usually control only one or two radiation types at a time, while space radiation combines galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events across a wide range of energies and particle types. A flown biosensor can record the biological response to the actual mixed environment, provided the measurement is paired with an in-flight radiation spectrometer; the BioSentinel design makes this pairing explicit [1][3]. Yeast is used as a simple, inexpensive model, but the value of any result depends on how well it transfers to the organism of concern. The sources reviewed do not yet include a published flight dataset that would confirm or refute the ground-based dose response [3][4].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a cellular radiation response experiment. Hardware ranges from ground assay equipment to dedicated CubeSat biosensors. The single example below is the best-documented flown case identified in this research. No second flown or flight-qualified example was verified from a primary source, so no comparative table is provided.

examples.name: BioSentinel biosensor on a 6U CubeSat
examples.type: Flown biological radiation biosensor (launched 16 November 2022 on Artemis I as a secondary payload) [1][2]
examples.form_factor: 6U CubeSat: a 2U solar-powered spacecraft bus and a 4U hermetically sealed aluminium biosensor enclosure [3]. NASA describes the spacecraft as shoebox-sized [2].
examples.organism: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (budding yeast), with a wild-type strain and a rad51-deletion strain that repairs double-strand DNA breaks poorly [1][3]
examples.biosensor: Two nine-card fluidic manifolds of microfluidic cards with 100 microlitre wells holding about 10^5 cells each; three-colour LED source and detector; metabolic indicator dye [1][3]
examples.radiation_sensor: TimePix-based LET spectrometer, developed with NASA Johnson Space Center, for linear energy transfer and total ionising dose [1][3]
examples.thermal_control: Heaters keep the payload at or above 4 degrees C; no active cooling [3]
examples.ground_reference_units: Identical payloads were built: one for the International Space Station and two as Earth-based controls [1]
examples.flight_status_notes: Flown. NASA's mission summary (last updated 31 July 2024) reports the spacecraft healthy and the science phase extended. The first yeast cards showed no growth, which NASA attributes to yeast expiring during long pre-launch storage rather than to radiation [1].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed beyond the 6U form factor and the split into a 2U bus and a 4U biosensor enclosure [3]. NASA's shoebox-sized description is qualitative [2]. No numerical external dimensions are recorded.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed, so no mass value is recorded. Mass would govern secondary-payload accommodation, but no accommodation or compatibility claim is made here.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power consumption is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The spacecraft bus is solar-powered [3], and NASA reports that batteries resumed recharging after a lunar eclipse following the flyby [2].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A flown cellular radiation experiment must survive launch, cruise and radiation in a sealed, thermally controlled environment. For BioSentinel, the sources describe a hermetically sealed biosensor enclosure, desiccated yeast, heaters that keep the payload at or above 4 degrees C without active cooling, and desiccant to control humidity [3]. Storage conditions matter: in ground tests, the best survival of dried yeast came from air-drying in 10% trehalose, storage at 0% relative humidity, or storage at 4-9 degrees C [3]. Operationally, the spacecraft tumbled shortly after launch; the team requested an emergency Deep Space Network pass and sent a detumble command, and telemetry confirmed recovery later that morning [2]. Yeast cards were activated at set points, and data were stored onboard and downlinked through the Deep Space Network [1].
article.limitations: This is a single-celled yeast model, not mammalian tissue or human cells. Flight outcomes are incomplete: the first yeast cards showed no growth, which NASA attributes to storage rather than radiation, and no peer-reviewed deep-space biology results were found in this research [1]. The 2023 Astrobiology paper was written before flight and reports ground data; mixed-ion (GCR/SPE) and transcriptomic results were deferred to later publications [3]. The ground dose-response data cover one particle type (1 GeV protons) and three dose levels [3]. The link to DNA repair is inferred rather than measured [3]. Mass, external dimensions and power consumption are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: BioSentinel was not a lunar-surface payload. It flew as one of ten CubeSats deployed from the Artemis I Space Launch System, passed the Moon on a lunar flyby, and was placed on a heliocentric trajectory [2][4]. This article therefore describes its deep-space integration rather than surface delivery. General lunar-surface delivery steps are discussed only where the sources support them.
transportation_process: Integrate the CubeSat as a secondary payload with the Artemis I launch vehicle [2].
Launch on the Space Launch System on 16 November 2022 [2].
Deploy from the launch vehicle as one of ten CubeSats; the deployer hardware and sequence are not described in the sources reviewed [2].
Recover attitude after an early tumble, confirmed by telemetry the same morning [2].
Perform a lunar flyby on 22 November 2022, about 250 miles above the surface, which supplied the energy needed to leave the Earth-Moon system [2][4].
Operate in heliocentric orbit, with yeast cards activated at set points [1][4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment was from the Artemis I launch vehicle as a secondary payload. The sources reviewed do not describe the deployer or the deployment mechanism [2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: BioSentinel is the flown example used in this article. NASA describes it as the first study of biological radiation response beyond low Earth orbit in almost 50 years [1]. No other flown or flight-qualified example of this payload class was verified from a primary source in this research.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted. For a future cellular radiation experiment, compatibility would depend on the sample system's mass, power, thermal control (the BioSentinel design relies on heaters and desiccant), radiation-sensor interfaces, and whether the experiment is a surface, orbital or deep-space payload. The BioSentinel design was a secondary CubeSat payload and is not a lunar-surface payload.

article.historical_significance: BioSentinel is significant as an attempt to measure a living organism's radiation response beyond low Earth orbit, with its ground-based dose-response work and flight design documented in a peer-reviewed paper and NASA sources [1][3]. The 2024 AIAA flight-dynamics paper records the mission's trajectory and navigation performance, which supports the flight record although it does not report biology results [4]. Its scientific value will depend on whether and when the flight biology data are published, which the sources reviewed do not report.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The BioSentinel NASA summary used here was last updated on 31 July 2024, so current mission status may differ [1]. No flight biological results were verified. The generic class name 'cellular radiation response experiment' does not correspond to one standard instrument, and no other flown or flight-qualified example was verified from a primary source. Mass, external dimensions and power are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Image rights follow NASA media terms; full-resolution downloads were not checked, and the second image's file metadata suggests a 2015 capture date [1][2].

data_quality_notes: The catalogue entry is a generic class. The article uses BioSentinel as the one flown, documented example; no other flown or flight-qualified example was verified from a primary source.
The BioSentinel organism is budding yeast (single-celled), not mammalian cell culture.
The NASA BioSentinel page at www.nasa.gov/biosentinel/ returned HTTP 404; the NASA Ames mission summary was used instead.
The NASA BioSentinel fact sheet (2019) and a 2006 COSPAR abstract on a proposed reporter-cell experiment were returned by search but could not be read as text; neither is cited.
Mass, external dimensions and power consumption for BioSentinel are not published in the sources reviewed; null values are recorded.
The microfluidic card photograph's embedded metadata gives a 2015 capture date while its upload path is 2023; it is used as a design illustration only.
Ground dose-response data (2023) were written before flight; no flight biology results were found.
A Chang'e 4 lunar-surface mini-biosphere experiment appeared in search results but is excluded: the reports were news items with conflicting accounts and no primary radiation-response data.
Search-result claims not confirmed by page reads (for example, NASA GeneLab datasets and NASA Space Radiation Laboratory cell-culture studies) are excluded from the article.
